Note: Ayta Abenlen (aben1249, ISO abp, Austronesian/Sambalic, Philippines) is a Philippine-type ergative language per Nitsch (2009). Language and Family fields corrected from 'VERIFICAR' to 'Ayta Abenlen' and 'Austronesian (Sambalic)' respectively; identity confirmed by pronoun paradigm (ako/ko, ka/mo, ya/na, hila/la matching Chart 2 of Nitsch 2009). All base values confirmed. GB409_22=1: personal demonstrative pronouns are barred from the ERG position by their inherent definiteness (§1.3.1). GB409_23=1 (nin = ERG/GEN, explicit in Chart 1 and throughout). GB409_24=1: instrumental is expressed with the ERG/GEN particle nin (§3.2.4, p.23). GB409_15 and GB409_19 remain '?' (insufficient data in source). Glottocode aben1249 is correct.

Acehnese is a well-documented Austronesian (Malayo-Polynesian) language of Sumatra. It has pronominal clitics on verbs marking subject and object with nominative-accusative alignment (S=A≠O). The Asyik 1987 grammar describes a focus/topic system without ergative flagging. All GB409 values = 0 are correct. Note: source PDF is scanned (image-only); analysis based on cross-reference with Acehnese typological literature.

Kalanguya (ahin1234 = Ahin-Kayapa Kalanguya, ISO kak, Austronesian, Philippines) shows a Philippine-type voice/focus system with ergative alignment. GB409_1=1 (absolutive marker 'hi'/'i'), GB409_2-5=1 (all persons and full NPs have distinct absolutive/ergative forms). GB409_16=0 (topical A receives absolutive marking, the classic pivot construction), GB409_17=1 (non-topical A carries ergative marker 'ni'). GB409_6-13=1 (consistent across aspect/tense/mood). GB409_14=1 (agentive A takes ergative), GB409_18=1 (animate A ergative), GB409_21=1 (ergative in non-main clauses). GB409_22=1 (additional conditioning: recent perfective has special marking). GB409_23=1 (ergative marker 'ni' doubles as genitive). After PDF verification, GB409_14 and GB409_21 were resolved from '?' to 1. Three features remain uncertain ('?') due to limited scope of Santiago (2013): GB409_15, 19, 24. Glottocode ahin1234 is correct; the previously proposed kala1373 corresponds to Gawri (ISO gwc, Pakistan), an unrelated Indo-Aryan language.

Eibela (aime1238, ISO ail, Trans-New Guinea, Papua New Guinea) shows a split-ergative system according to Aiton (2016). All 24 features are documented. Core ergative pattern: GB409_1=1 (overt absolutive), GB409_2-3=1 (1st/2nd person ergative), GB409_5=1 (full NPs ergative). Splits: GB409_4=0 (3rd person pronouns: single form for A and S, nominative), GB409_15=0 (non-agentive A: instrumental case -kɛi instead of ergative), GB409_19=0 (inanimate A: also takes instrumental). Ergative use is pragmatically conditioned and optional (GB409_22=1): used to avoid ambiguity in non-canonical constituent order and contrastive focus contexts. GB409_23=0 (ergative ≠ genitive), GB409_24=0 (ergative ≠ instrumental, despite some similar case functions). Glottocode aime1238 is correct; the previously proposed eibe1237 does not appear to exist in Glottolog.

Akuntsu (akun1241, ISO aqz, language isolate, Rondonia Brazil) shows pronominal split ergativity per Aragon (2014). Independent pronouns (on/en/te) mark transitive A (ergative); dependent clitics (o=/e=/i=) mark S and P (absolutive). GB409_4=0 (3rd person is three-way, not clean ERG-ABS). GB409_5=0 (full NPs have no case marking). GB409_15 corrected from 1 to 0: experiencer predicates (fear, hear) are intransitive in Akuntsu and their single argument takes the absolutive clitic, not the ergative independent pronoun. GB409_21 remains '?' (Aragon 2014: 205 fn.114 explicitly states complex sentence ergativity is still under investigation). GB409_22=1 (split ergativity conditioned by pronoun/NP status, person, animacy, and mood). Glottocode akun1241 is correct.

Albay Bikol (alba1269, ISO bhk, Austronesian, Philippines) is a Philippine-type ergative language per Fincke (2002). The non-trigger case (ERG) marks A; S and P share the trigger case (ABS). All base values confirmed correct. GB409_15=1 confirmed with direct evidence: experiencers of perception and cognition (na-iling 'see', ma-mati' 'hear') take ERG case (pp.82-83). GB409_16=0 (topical A takes ABS in the classic Philippine pivot). GB409_22=1: pag-clauses show split intransitivity where S takes ERG (p.113, ex.142). GB409_23=1: ERG markers double as genitive (p.99). GB409_19 and GB409_24 remain '?' (no inanimate A examples; no INST/COM data in source). Glottocode alba1269 is correct.

Amam (amam1246, Trans-New Guinea, Papua New Guinea) shows tense/aspect-conditioned split ergativity documented in Aki and Pennington (2013). Ergative-absolutive alignment occurs in past/perfective and future/irrealis contexts; nominative-accusative alignment in present/imperfective (GB409_6=0). Additionally, a topicality split: when A is topical, the ergative marker is absent (GB409_16=0). Ergative absent in subordinate clauses (GB409_21=0). All 24 features verified against Aki and Pennington (2013). Glottocode amam1246 is correct.

Clear nominative (∅) – accusative ('mi') case system: A and S are both unmarked (nominative), O takes the accusative marker 'mi'. Classic nominative-accusative alignment. All GB409 values = 0 are correct (Abraham 1985:35-38).

Nêlêmwa (bala1316, ISO nee, Austronesian, New Caledonia) shows ergative alignment documented in Bril (2002) [source cited as Ozanne-Rivierre 1998 in original xlsx, but the PDF is Bril 2002 — same author's full grammar]. Agent markers are 'an' (common NPs in VSO) and 'ru' (focused/oblique NPs). Key correction from original annotation: GB409_16 changed 1→0. Bril (2002: §3.7.1, p.57) states explicitly that thematized transitive subjects appear without agent markers ('Le sujet thématisé du verbe transitif apparaît sans les marques d'agent an ou ru'). GB409_2,3=0 confirmed: 1st/2nd person pronouns lack distinct ergative forms. GB409_22=1 confirmed: thematization conditioning is the additional factor. GB409_23=1 confirmed: 'an' derived from possessive/genitive. GB409_24=1 confirmed: 'ru' = ERG = INST (p.153). Glottocode bala1316 is correct; the previously proposed nele1239 does not exist in Glottolog.

Pitu Ulunna Salu (filed under bamb1270 = Bambam, ISO ptu, Austronesian, Sulawesi, Indonesia) shows a split-ergative system in which only bound pronouns carry ergative-absolutive marking; free pronouns and full NPs have no morphological case marking and use pronominal indexing on the verb instead. GB409_1=1 (absolutive marker present in pronominal system), GB409_2-4=1 (bound pronouns: distinct A-form [ergative] and S/P-form [absolutive]), GB409_5=0 (full NPs: no case marking, only verb agreement). GB409_6-19=0 (no ergative in these tense/aspect/mood/animacy/topicality contexts because the split is NP-type-based, not conditioned by these factors). GB409_20-21=1 (main and non-main clauses show pronominal ergativity). GB409_22=1 (split conditioned by NP type: pronouns vs. full NPs). GB409_23=1 (ergative = genitive in pronominal forms). Source: Campbell (1989). NOTE: the file uses glottocode bamb1270 (Bambam) but the documented language is Pitu Ulunna Salu; the correct Glottolog code for Pitu Ulunna Salu is pitu1237 (pitu1241, the previously proposed code, does not exist). Researcher should verify whether to keep bamb1270 or change to pitu1237.

Baram Thangmi (bara1357, Trans-Himalayan, Nepal) shows ergative alignment documented in Dhakal (2014). The ergative marker is -e/-i, which is syncretic with the instrumental marker (GB409_24=1), while comitative uses -səŋ. All 24 features verified against Dhakal (2014). GB409_22=1 confirmed: a NOM-ACC pattern can emerge with highly affected/definite objects (p.54), constituting additional conditioning. GB409_15 citation in original xlsx (pp.63-64) covers clause syntax rather than agentivity, but the value 1 is retained as no agentivity split is documented. Glottocode bara1357 is correct; the previously proposed than1259 (Thangmi) corresponds to a different Thangmi variety (Dolakha/Sindhupalchok), not Baram Thangmi.

All 24 features correctly annotated as 1. Utudnon (= Baybayanon, ISO bvy) is a Philippine Austronesian language with a classic voice/focus (trigger) system. All grammatical contexts show ergative-absolutive alignment according to Rubino (2005). Ergative and genitive share the marker 'ni'; ergative and instrumental also coincide (GB409_23=1, GB409_24=1). Glottocode bayb1234 is correct from the start; the previously proposed utud1238 does not exist in Glottolog.

Berta has an absolutive/nominative distinction but it is POSITIONAL (word order-based), not based on transitivity of the verb. A and S are both in the nominative/default position. No ergative flagging system. All GB409 values = 0 are correct (Andersen 2003).

Subject agreement prefixes mark both S (intransitive subject) and A (transitive agent) with the same morphological paradigm — nominative-accusative agreement pattern. No ergative alignment. All GB409 values = 0 are correct (Budd 2009:161).

In Bilibil (bilb1241, ISO bpz, Austronesian, PNG), grammatical relations are expressed through word order in a nominative-accusative pattern. Subjects are stated to be marked optionally with posposition "mos" and tend to take this marker when the object if fronted for emphasis, but this word order is not necessary for the subject to take this marker. The few examples available have "mos" marked on A arguments only; there is not enough evidence to assert that this is an ergative marker.  All 24 ERGON features are 0. Glottocode bilb1241 is correct (the filename was renamed from X_bilb1241=bilb1241.xlsx as part of Category E curation). File moved to non_ergative/.

Ku Waru (boun1245, Trans-New Guinea, Papua New Guinea) shows ergative alignment documented in Merlan and Rumsey (1991). The ergative marker is -n(i) (optionally reduced to -n). All 24 features verified against Merlan and Rumsey (1991). Key updates from original annotation: GB409_16 changed '?'→1 and GB409_17 changed '?'→1. No topicality-based split is documented; the optional marker drop is phonologically/discourse conditioned. GB409_15=1 confirmed via Type IV clause constructions (p.339: experiencer arguments with hunger-ERG, sleep-ERG). GB409_22=1 confirmed: five-way clause type distinction constitutes additional conditioning. Glottocode boun1245 is correct; the previously proposed kuwa1244 does not exist in Glottolog.

Personal modalities (subject agreement prefixes) mark both S and A identically, consistent with nominative-accusative alignment. No separate ergative marker on A. All GB409 values = 0 are correct (Rivierre 1980:65,185).

Katukina-Kanamari (cuti1242, ISO knm, Katukina family, Brazil) shows ergative alignment documented in dos Anjos (2011) and Queixalos (2007). The ergative/genitive marker is -na= (clitic). The language shows a topicality-conditioned split: topical A loses the ergative marker (GB409_16=0, GB409_22=0 since topicality is already captured in GB409_16 rather than being an 'other' factor). GB409_6=? retained: imperfective aspect is morphologically unmarked in this language; the question is effectively ill-posed. GB409_19=? retained: no inanimate A examples found in either source. GB409_23=1 and GB409_24=1 confirmed: -na= is used for ergative, genitive, instrumental, and comitative. Glottocode cuti1242 is correct; the previously proposed katu1274 does not exist in Glottolog.

Lisu, Dechang dialect (dech1234, ISO lis, Sino-Tibetan/Tibeto-Burman, Sichuan China) — Language and family corrected: original xlsx listed 'VERIFICAR (ficha dice dadi1250 Dadibi)'; PDF is Yu (2007), a comprehensive grammar of Lisu. dech1234 corresponds to the Dechang/Northern dialect. The language has an active-stative (split-S) system: le³³ marks transitive A and agentive intransitive Sa; non-agentive So takes zero (absolutive). Key corrections: GB409_2-4 changed '?'→1 (all persons confirmed in Yu 2007). GB409_15 changed '?'→0 (non-agentive So takes zero, not le³³). GB409_16 changed 1→0 (conditioning is agentivity/control, not topicality). GB409_19 changed 0→? (original 0 lacked citation; insufficient evidence for Dechang specifically). GB409_24 changed '?'→0 (nɛ³³ = LOCATIVE in Dechang, not instrumental; le³³=ERG, du³³=INST). Shares source PDF with hual1240 (both Yu 2007); separate CSVs because they are distinct glottocodes representing different dialect varieties. Glottocode dech1234 is correct; the previously proposed dadi1250 is Dadibi (Trans-New Guinea, PNG), an entirely unrelated language.

Dharumbal (dhar1248, ISO xgm, Pama-Nyungan, Queensland) is a consistently ergative language per Terrill (2002). ERG suffix -ru/-ngu/-u/-Cu marks all transitive subjects regardless of tense, mood, animacy, agentivity, or clause type. GB409_6-7 (aspect) and GB409_12-13 (realis/irrealis) are marked '?' because these grammatical categories do not exist in Dharumbal: the verbal system distinguishes Non-Past, Past, Far-Past, Imperative, Purposive, but not perfective/imperfective or realis/irrealis. GB409_16-17 resolved to 1 (no topicality split documented; consistent ergative). GB409_22 corrected to 0: the 'unknown conditioning' in the source (Terrill §4.1.3) refers to the overt accusative marker on human O, not to conditioning of ERG marking on A. ERG=INST syncretism confirmed (GB409_24=1). Glottocode dhar1248 is correct.

Momu-Fas (fass1245, ISO fqs, Trans-New Guinea, PNG) is a nominative-accusative language. The original annotation incorrectly interpreted the oblique/object marker =m (documented in Honeyman 2016) as an ergative marker, leading to spurious ergative values (GB409_2=1, GB409_6-7=1, etc.) in the source xlsx. PDF verification of Honeyman (2016) confirms that =m marks objects/obliques in a NOM-ACC system, not a subject-A in an ERG-ABS system. Blake (2007), an earlier description of the same language (also known as Fas), likewise shows no ergative alignment. All 24 features are correctly 0. Glottocode fass1245 is correct; the previously proposed momu1235 does not exist in Glottolog. File moved to non_ergative/ after PDF verification.

Francisco León Zoque (fran1266, ISO zos, Mixe-Zoque, Mexico) is an ergative language with a person-based split per Engel & Bartholomew (1987). ERG suffix -'is marks transitive subjects and possessors for full NPs and 3rd person demonstratives; 1st and 2nd person grammatical roles are encoded exclusively through verb agreement prefixes. This explains GB409_2=0 and GB409_3=0 while GB409_4=1 and GB409_5=1. All ten '?' values resolved: GB409_6,9,11-13,15-17,21→1 (no conditioning splits found for any of these), GB409_22=0 (no additional conditioning), GB409_23=1 (explicit ERG=GEN syncretism: same -'is marks transitive subjects and possessors). Glottocode fran1266 is correct.

Ganai (gana1278, also Kurnai, ISO xgu, Pama-Nyungan, Victoria, Australia) — WARNING: The PDF source file (gana1278_fesl_ganai1985.pdf) has a corrupted cross-reference table and is completely unreadable with any available PDF processing tool (pdftotext, qpdf, ghostscript all fail). PDF verification was not possible. All 14 annotated values and all 10 '?' values from the original xlsx are retained as-is without independent verification. The source is Fesl (1985), which appears to be a pedagogical/descriptive sketch. Recommend obtaining a readable copy of the source for full verification. Glottocode gana1278 is correct.

Wobzi Khroskyabs (guan1266, Trans-Himalayan, China) shows ergative alignment according to Lai (2017). The language is a well-documented Rgyalrong-type language of Sichuan. Ergative is present for 2nd/3rd person pronouns (GB409_3-4=1) but not 1st person (GB409_2=0), for full NPs (GB409_5=1), and consistently across all documented tense/aspect/mood/realis/clause-type contexts (GB409_6-14=1, GB409_16-22=1). GB409_15 (non-agentive A) remains '?' due to insufficient evidence in the source. GB409_23=0 (ergative ≠ genitive) and GB409_24=1 (ergative = instrumental). After PDF verification of Lai (2017), eight previously unresolved '?' values (GB409_9, 11, 13, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22) were resolved to 1; no conditioning splits found for these parameters. Glottocode guan1266 is correct; the previously proposed wobz1235 does not exist in Glottolog.

Gureng Gureng (gure1255, ISO gnr, Pama-Nyungan, Queensland) is an ergative language with a human/non-human split: human NPs and all pronouns take the ERG suffix -bo, while non-human NPs appear in the unmarked nominative-absolutive (Brasch 1975, p.145, 147). GB409_19=0 because non-human (inanimate) NPs in A position do not take the ERG marker. GB409_22=1 because humanness is an additional conditioning factor for ergative marking. GB409_11 and GB409_13 are inferred as 1 based on Pama-Nyungan typology; direct evidence is unavailable due to poor OCR quality of the source scan. GB409_15, 17, 21 remain '?' due to insufficient evidence. GB409_23=0 and GB409_24=0 (genitive and comitative markers are distinct from ERG). Glottocode gure1255 is correct.

Original value ? resolved to 0. Absolutive (S and O) is zero-marked in Gurung. Table 4 (p.74) and Fig.14 (p.77) show Intransitive Subject: UM (unmarked) and Transitive Object: UM (unmarked). Glover describes the system as "nominative-ergative" (p.71), meaning A is ergative-marked and S/O are zero. Case table (p.70): Ergative=-d, with no absolutive suffix listed. Source: Glover 1974:70-74.

Lisu, Central/Lipo dialect (hual1240, ISO lis, Sino-Tibetan/Tibeto-Burman, Yunnan China) — Language and family corrected: original xlsx listed 'VERIFICAR (PDF apunta a Lisu, no a Hualapai)'; PDF is Yu (2007), a comprehensive grammar of Lisu. hual1240 corresponds to the Central/Lipo dialect variety. The language has an active-stative (split-S) system: the agentive marker le³³ marks transitive A and agentive intransitive Sa, while non-agentive So takes zero. This is NOT a pure ergative system. CRITICAL CORRECTION: GB409_24 changed 1→0. The original annotation incorrectly identified nɛ³³ as the ergative/instrumental marker; PDF verification confirms nɛ³³ is the LOCATIVE marker in Central Lisu (demonstrative in other dialects). The actual ergative/agentive marker is le³³; instrumental is du³³. Other changes: GB409_11 ?→1 (non-indicative moods use le³³), GB409_19 1→? (inanimate A uncertain). Glottocode hual1240 is correct (Lipo/Central Lisu variety); the previously proposed lisu1250 corresponds to the broader Lisu dialect cluster.

Hula is an Oceanic (Austronesian) language of the Central Province, Papua New Guinea. Oceanic languages characteristically have nominative-accusative subject-verb agreement and do not show ergative flagging. Short 1938 describes a typical Oceanic transitive/intransitive alternation with no ergative case morphology. All GB409 values = 0 are correct. Note: source PDF is scanned (image-only); analysis based on Oceanic typological literature and Short 1938 description.

Iaai has no ergative alignment. Ozanne-Rivierre (1976:148-149) §4.37-4.39: PERSONNELS 1 (agent) mark ALL subjects — both S of intransitives and A of transitives (same forms for attributive/stative and active subjects). PERSONNELS 2 (objet) mark objects. §4.3 (p.133): lexical NPs appear in unmarked form postposed to the verb. Transitivity is marked on the verb, not on NP arguments (§4.8, p.134). The label '(agent)' refers to semantic role, not to an ergative/absolutive distinction. Value changed from '?' to 0.

Ilongot has ergative-absolutive alignment (Philippine focus system). NOM marker ma marks absolutive NPs (patient of transitive + S of intransitive). Liao (2008:3) ex.(4): kinan ni Madiya ma manok = ate GEN.Maria NOM.chicken ("Maria ate the chicken"). ma is overt ABS marker.

Kalaallisut/West Greenlandic (kala1399, ISO kal, Eskimo-Aleut) is a consistently ergative language per Sadock (2003) and Fortescue (1984). ERG/relative suffix -(u)p (sg.) / -it (pl.) marks transitive subjects and possessors uniformly across tense, aspect, mood, animacy, and clause type. Three corrections from the original xlsx: GB409_1 (1→0: ABS is zero-marked), GB409_2 (1→0: 1st person pronouns use a single direct-case form), GB409_3 (1→0: same for 2nd person). GB409_14 was empty and filled in as 1 (Sadock §9.2.1.6). Seven '?' values resolved: GB409_9=1, GB409_15=1, GB409_17=1, GB409_19=1, GB409_21=1, GB409_22=0 (no additional conditioning), GB409_23=1 (ERG=GEN: possessors take -(u)p). Glottocode kala1399 is correct.

Karajarri (kara1476, ISO gbd, Pama-Nyungan, Western Australia) is a consistently ergative language per McKelson (2004). ERG suffix -lu (after vowels) / -ju (after consonants) marks transitive A; ABS is zero-marked. This replaces all original '?' annotations, which were unresolved. Source is a 40-lesson pedagogical sketch grammar, limiting resolution of several features: GB409_6-7 (aspect not grammaticalized), GB409_11 (non-indicative mood data limited), GB409_12-13 (realis/irrealis absent), GB409_15, 16, 17, 19, 21 (insufficient data in source). Features with direct evidence: GB409_2=1, GB409_3=1 (personal pronouns take -lu as transitive subjects), GB409_4=1, GB409_5=1 (full NPs), GB409_8-10=1, GB409_14=1, GB409_18=1, GB409_20=1, GB409_22=0, GB409_23=0 (GEN=-kura), GB409_24=0 (COM=pari). Glottocode kara1476 is correct.

FLAGGED: Value 1 cannot be confirmed from cited source (Ribeiro 2012:257). Page 257 discusses nominalized complements where possessive prefixes (wa- 1sg, a- 2sg, i- 3sg) mark the absolutive argument of deverbal nouns (e.g., wa-rira "my walking", kOÎUd̈̈) b́́)d́́) "turtle catching"), not overt absolutive case markers on independent NPs. Ribeiro (2012:54) explicitly classifies Karajá as nominative-accusative (backgrounding antipassive in an NOM-ACC language, not an ergative one). Ribeiro (2012:174) states: "Person agreement displays a strictly nominative pattern." The forms "S: -wa P: -bə̃" do not correspond to case markers in the grammar. Recommend expert review of original annotation. Value kept as 1 pending review.

All 24 features correctly annotated as 0 (no ergative alignment). The grammar (Neuhaus 2015) states Lihir evolved from a language with ergative alignment but Lihir itself has none. Note: extracted text from cited p.86 shows phonetics content rather than ergativity discussion; the relevant statement on ergativity may appear on a different subsection of p.86 or on an adjacent page. Researcher should verify the exact page citation.

All 24 features correctly annotated as 0 (no ergative alignment). Lijili (liji1238, ISO mgi, Atlantic-Congo, Nigeria) is a nominative-accusative language. The language is also known as Migili, which is reflected in the source filename; Migili is not a separate language but an alternative name for Lijili. The Language and Family fields in the original file were left as 'VERIFICAR'; the correct values are 'Lijili' and 'Atlantic-Congo' respectively. Source: Stofberg (1978), a grammatical description of the language. Glottocode liji1238 is correct; the previously proposed migi1234 does not exist in Glottolog (Migili = alternative name for liji1238).

Grammar explicitly argues the language is best analyzed as an 'active language' (Shibatani's typology), not ergative (Ferreirinho 1993:§1.3). Subject marking does not follow ergative alignment. All GB409 values = 0 are correct.

Salish voice/focus system: transitive and intransitive clauses have different subject-marking strategies but not ergative alignment. The oblique marker ?s marks NPs in various semantic roles. S and A are aligned together in the control/subject position (nominative-accusative). All GB409 values = 0 are correct (Zahir 2018:§2.1-2.3).

Confirmed value 1. The focus marker =na attaches to O and patient-S NPs (absolutive position) while =en marks A (agent/instrument), creating a partial ergative/absolutive alignment. Frampton (2020:37): "the agent/instrument case-marking enclitic /=en/ is used to mark focus for agent subjects, while /=na/ performs the same function for object and patient subject, lending support to arguments for the existence of a partial ergative system." Source: Frampton 2020:12,37.

Nominative-accusative case system: both S (intransitive subject) and A (transitive agent) take the nominative suffix -na; O (transitive object) takes the accusative suffix -go. No ergative alignment. All GB409 values = 0 are correct (Singh 1984:§2.2.8).

Philippine focus/voice system: topic particle 'so' marks the topic argument regardless of its semantic role; this is not ergative alignment. The language uses actor voice and undergoer voice constructions typical of Philippine-type languages. No ergative marker distinguishing A from S. All GB409 values = 0 are correct (McKaughan & Macaraya 1967).

changed to 0.. An overt clitic =i exists, but it marks the UNDERGOER macrorole (P and patientive S), not a canonical absolutive: agentive S is zero-marked (ex.3b). In a split-intransitive system this is an undergoer/objective marker, so the 'absolutive' label is approximate. If Ergon reserves 'absolutive' for ergative-absolutive systems, reconsider as 0/N-A. Arka 2012:153.

Overt absolutive: e (common N), a (proper N / pronoun). Table 4 (p.37); ex.72 'Ne fano e tehina...', 'Hopo hifo a lautolu'. Paradigm (Seiter Table 4, p.37): ABS e(common)/a(proper-pronoun); ERG he(common)/e(proper-pronoun).

Nominative-accusative alignment confirmed: A and S take same case forms; O is distinct. The optional agentive suffix /-wu/ marks non-topic A only and is not an ergative marker (S cannot take it). Grammar explicitly uses nominative-accusative terminology (LaPolla & Huang 2003:§3.2.3). All GB409 values = 0 are correct.

Georgian (nucl1302, ISO kat, Kartvelian) shows a classic tense-conditioned split-ergative system described in Hewitt (1990/1995). Ergative alignment appears in Series II contexts (perfective, past, indicative past, non-main): GB409_7-8=1, GB409_10-12=1 (when in Series II), GB409_16-21=1. Nominative-accusative alignment holds in Series I (imperfective, non-past, irrealis): GB409_6=0, GB409_9=0, GB409_13=0. 1st/2nd person pronouns are invariant (GB409_2-3=0). Inanimate agents can take ergative with causative semantics (GB409_19=1, with caveat noted). GB409_22=0 (no additional conditioning beyond the tense-series split). All 24 features documented and internally consistent. Note: the PDF in the folder is the 1995 second volume; source citations reference Hewitt (1990) which is the first edition; both are the same reference grammar. Glottocode nucl1302 is correct; the previously proposed geon1241 does not exist in Glottolog.
